speakerBio: Dual-trained hepatologist and intensivist who teaches that the INR in a cirrhotic is a trap, and that most special-population bleeds are lost to the reflex, not the disease.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

Three patients arrive on the same night. A 55-year-old with cirrhosis is bleeding and his INR is 2.4 — the registrar reaches for FFP. An 80-year-old with severe aortic stenosis has her fourth admission this year for iron-deficiency melaena and "normal-ish" scopes. A dialysis patient oozes from every puncture site with a normal INR and normal platelet count. Three bleeds, three completely different mechanisms — and in each one, the "obvious" reflex (transfuse plasma, cauterise and forget, transfuse platelets) is the wrong move. Special populations break the standard rules, and tonight we rewrite them.

1 · 🫀 Cirrhosis — rebalanced haemostasis, not "auto-anticoagulated"

The single most damaging myth in hepatology is that a cirrhotic with a raised INR is "auto-anticoagulated" and bleeds because their blood won't clot. This is wrong. Cirrhosis produces a rebalanced haemostasis: the liver makes less of the pro-coagulant factors (II, VII, IX, X — hence the high INR) but also less of the anticoagulant proteins (protein C, protein S, antithrombin), and von Willebrand factor is markedly elevated. The system re-equilibrates at a lower, more fragile set-point that can tip either way — cirrhotics get portal vein thrombosis and DVT as well as bleeding.

⚠️ The INR does NOT predict bleeding in cirrhosis

The INR was validated to monitor warfarin, not to measure global haemostasis in liver disease. It reflects only the pro-coagulant factors and is blind to the parallel fall in anticoagulants. A cirrhotic with an INR of 2.5 is not "anticoagulated." Do not transfuse FFP to chase the INR before procedures — it rarely corrects the number, volume-loads the portal system (raising portal pressure and bleeding risk), and exposes the patient to TACO/TRALI. Prophylactic FFP for a number is a harm, not a treatment.

What actually matters in the bleeding or pre-procedure cirrhotic:

  • Fibrinogen — a low fibrinogen (<1.0–1.5 g/L) is a genuine, correctable bleeding risk; replace with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate if bleeding.
  • Platelets — thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism/low thrombopoietin matters; but the threshold to transfuse is low, and thrombopoietin-receptor agonists (avatrombopag, lusutrombopag) can raise counts before elective procedures, avoiding transfusion.
  • Viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) — reflects global clot formation far better than INR and reduces unnecessary blood-product use in bleeding cirrhotics.
  • Portal pressure — for variceal bleeding, lowering portal pressure (vasoactive drugs, band ligation) does far more than any clotting-factor top-up.
In cirrhosis, treat the fibrinogen and the platelets and the portal pressure — never the INR. The number lies.

2 · 🌊 Heyde syndrome — the valve that bleeds through the gut

A beautiful, curable mechanism-story. In severe aortic stenosis (and in LVADs), blood is forced through a narrow, high-shear orifice. The high shear unfolds and cleaves the largest, most haemostatically active von Willebrand factor multimers (by the protease ADAMTS13), producing an acquired type 2A von Willebrand syndrome. Those large multimers are exactly what you need to plug bleeding from fragile vessels — so the patient develops bleeding from GI angiodysplasia, which is itself more common in aortic stenosis. The triad: aortic stenosis (or LVAD) + GI angiodysplasia + acquired vWF deficiency.

💡 The cure is mechanical, not haematological

Endoscopic ablation of angiodysplasia in Heyde syndrome often fails because the lesions are multiple and the vWF defect persists. Aortic valve replacement (surgical or TAVI) reverses the shear, restores the large vWF multimers, and durably stops the bleeding — and LVAD-associated bleeding likewise tracks the shear. Fix the valve/pump and you fix the gut.

3 · 🫘 CKD / uraemic platelet dysfunction — normal count, broken platelets

In advanced CKD, uraemic toxins impair platelet function (adhesion and aggregation, via defective platelet–vWF interaction and nitric-oxide-mediated inhibition) — the platelet count and INR are normal, but the platelets don't work. Bleeding time is prolonged; the patient oozes from puncture sites, GI angiodysplasia, and mucosa.

InterventionHow it helpsNote
Desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.3 µg/kg IVReleases vWF/FVIII from endothelium → improves platelet adhesion; works within ~1 hFirst-line acute rescue; tachyphylaxis after 1–2 doses; watch for hyponatraemia
DialysisClears uraemic toxins, partially restoring platelet functionThe definitive underlying fix
Correct anaemia (Hb ~100)Red cells push platelets to the vessel wall (rheology)EPO / transfusion
Cryoprecipitate / conjugated oestrogensSupply vWF / longer-lasting effect (oestrogens act over days)Second-line for refractory or recurrent bleeding

Platelet transfusion is largely ineffective here — the transfused platelets become dysfunctional in the uraemic milieu. Desmopressin, dialysis, and correcting anaemia are the levers.

4 · 🔧 Anticoagulated mechanical valves who bleed

The hardest balance in medicine: a mechanical valve mandates anticoagulation, yet the patient is bleeding. Full, prolonged reversal risks fatal valve thrombosis; under-treatment risks exsanguination. The approach: reverse warfarin only as far as needed for life-threatening bleeding (4F-PCC + IV vitamin K, and keep vitamin K modest to avoid prolonged resistance to re-warfarinisation), secure endoscopic haemostasis, and bridge back early with a heparin infusion that can be stopped in seconds if bleeding recurs. These patients cannot be left off anticoagulation for long — mitral and older-generation valves are especially unforgiving.

5 · 👵 The frail elderly

Older patients concentrate every risk: polypharmacy (NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants, SSRIs), angiodysplasia, comorbid cardiac/renal disease that narrows the transfusion window, and poorer physiological reserve. They tolerate both hypovolaemia and over-transfusion badly. Principles: a genuinely restrictive transfusion strategy (target Hb ~70 g/L, ~80 with cardiac ischaemia), meticulous review to stop the culprit drugs, low threshold to co-prescribe a PPI, and realistic, ceiling-of-care conversations — endoscopy and its risks must be justified against frailty and goals of care.

6 · 🤰 GI bleeding in pregnancy (brief)

Uncommon but distinctive. The dominant upper-GI cause is Mallory–Weiss tears from hyperemesis gravidarum; reflux/gastritis is common, peptic ulcers are actually less frequent (progesterone effects). Management: endoscopy is safe in pregnancy when indicated (left-lateral tilt, minimise sedation, avoid unnecessary radiation), PPIs are considered safe, and iron for anaemia. In known portal hypertension, variceal bleeding is highest in the second/third trimester — band ligation is preferred, and non-selective beta-blockers are used with fetal monitoring. Always involve obstetrics.

7 · 🫁 Stress-related mucosal bleeding in the critically ill

The critically ill develop stress-related mucosal disease from splanchnic hypoperfusion and mucosal ischaemia. But clinically important stress-ulcer bleeding is now uncommon (good resuscitation and early enteral feeding protect the mucosa), so blanket prophylaxis is both unnecessary and harmful. The task is to prophylax the right patients and spare the rest.

🎯 Who actually needs stress-ulcer prophylaxis?

The two strongest, evidence-based indications are mechanical ventilation (≥48 h) and coagulopathy (platelets <50, INR >1.5, or aPTT >2× normal). Other risk factors: shock, high-dose steroids with another risk factor, severe burns, traumatic brain/spinal injury, and prior GI bleeding. A patient with none of these — and especially one tolerating enteral feed — usually does not need prophylaxis.

⚠️ The harms of over-prophylaxis

Acid suppression is not free. Raising gastric pH allows bacterial overgrowth and is associated with ventilator-associated / hospital-acquired pneumonia and Clostridioides difficile infection. In low-risk patients, blanket PPI/H2-blocker prophylaxis can cause more harm (infection) than the bleeding it prevents. The large PEPTIC and SUP-ICU trials found the mortality difference between PPIs, H2-blockers, and even placebo in appropriately selected populations to be small — reinforcing that prophylaxis should be targeted and stopped as soon as the risk factors resolve (e.g. extubation, feeding established). PPIs are somewhat more effective at preventing bleeding than H2-blockers but carry the infection trade-off.

8 · 📋 Scenario → mechanism → specific action

ScenarioMechanismSpecific action (and what NOT to do)

☠️ M&M — the plasma that raised the pressure

A 58-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis and known oesophageal varices presented with a small haematemesis. His INR was 2.6, and — anchored on the number — the team transfused four units of FFP "to correct the coagulopathy" before endoscopy, plus liberal red cells to a haemoglobin of 105. The FFP did not budge the INR. What it did do was expand his plasma volume and drive up his portal pressure; forty minutes later he had a torrential variceal bleed, aspirated, and arrested. Lessons: the INR does not measure bleeding risk in cirrhosis, and FFP given to chase it is not benign — the volume load raises portal pressure and can precipitate the catastrophic variceal bleed you were trying to prevent. The right moves were vasoactive drugs (terlipressin) and prophylactic antibiotics up front, a restrictive transfusion target of ~70 g/L, and urgent band ligation — treating the portal pressure and the fibrinogen, never the INR. He was killed by the correction, not the coagulopathy.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Cirrhosis is rebalanced, not auto-anticoagulated — the INR lies; treat fibrinogen, platelets, and portal pressure, and do not transfuse FFP to chase the number.
  2. Heyde syndrome (aortic stenosis/LVAD + angiodysplasia + acquired vWD from high shear) is cured by fixing the valve/pump, not by endless ablation.
  3. Uraemic bleeding is a platelet-function defect with a normal count — reach for desmopressin, dialysis, and correcting anaemia, not platelet transfusion.
  4. Mechanical valves that bleed get minimal-necessary reversal, endoscopic control, and an early heparin bridge — never a prolonged anticoagulation holiday.
  5. The frail elderly need restrictive transfusion, culprit-drug review, and honest goals-of-care.
  6. Pregnancy: think Mallory–Weiss from hyperemesis; endoscopy and PPIs are safe; band-ligate varices.
  7. Stress-ulcer prophylaxis is for the ventilated and the coagulopathic — everyone else risks pneumonia and C. diff for no benefit. Prophylax narrowly, stop early.

moderatorQs.q: A bleeding cirrhotic has an INR of 2.5. Why is transfusing FFP to correct it before endoscopy usually the wrong move?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because the INR does not measure bleeding risk in cirrhosis. Liver disease produces a rebalanced haemostasis: the pro-coagulant factors are low (raising the INR) but so are the anticoagulant proteins — protein C, protein S, antithrombin — which the INR cannot see, and vWF is actually elevated. So an INR of 2.5 does not mean 'anticoagulated'. Transfusing FFP rarely corrects the number, and worse, the volume load raises portal pressure and can precipitate variceal bleeding, plus TACO/TRALI risk. The things that genuinely matter are fibrinogen (replace if <1.0–1.5 g/L with bleeding), platelet count, and portal pressure — guided ideally by viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM). For variceal bleeding, vasoactive drugs, antibiotics, and band ligation do far more than any plasma.

moderatorQs.q: An 80-year-old with severe aortic stenosis has recurrent iron-deficiency GI bleeding and multiple angiodysplasias. What is the definitive treatment?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: This is Heyde syndrome, and the definitive treatment is aortic valve replacement (surgical or TAVI), not repeated endoscopic ablation. The mechanism is elegant: severe aortic stenosis creates a high-shear jet that unfolds and lets ADAMTS13 cleave the largest von Willebrand factor multimers — the very ones needed to plug bleeding from fragile vessels — producing an acquired type 2A von Willebrand syndrome, while angiodysplasia (itself commoner in AS) provides the fragile vessels. Because the lesions are multiple and the vWF defect persists, ablation alone tends to fail and the patient keeps re-bleeding. Replacing the valve removes the shear, restores the large vWF multimers, and durably stops the bleeding. The same shear logic applies to LVAD-associated GI bleeding.

moderatorQs.q: Which critically ill patients actually need stress-ulcer prophylaxis, and what is the downside of giving it to everyone?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The two strongest evidence-based indications are invasive mechanical ventilation (≥48 h) and coagulopathy (platelets <50, INR >1.5, or aPTT >2× normal); other risk factors include shock, high-dose steroids plus another risk factor, major burns, and severe neurotrauma. Clinically important stress-ulcer bleeding is now uncommon because good resuscitation and early enteral feeding protect the mucosa, so a patient with none of those risk factors — especially one tolerating feed — usually needs no prophylaxis. The downside of blanket prophylaxis is real: acid suppression raises gastric pH, promoting bacterial overgrowth linked to ventilator-associated pneumonia and C. difficile infection. The discipline is to prophylax narrowly and stop as soon as the risk factors resolve — at extubation or once feeding is established.

audienceQs.q: My dialysis patient is oozing everywhere but the platelet count and INR are normal. What do I give?
audienceQs.answerHTML: This is uraemic platelet dysfunction — the count is normal but the platelets don't adhere or aggregate properly, so transfusing platelets doesn't help (they too become dysfunctional in the uraemic milieu). The fast acute rescue is desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.3 µg/kg IV, which releases vWF and factor VIII from endothelium and improves platelet adhesion within about an hour — but expect tachyphylaxis after one or two doses and watch for hyponatraemia. Alongside it: dialyse to clear the uraemic toxins (the underlying fix), correct the anaemia to a haemoglobin around 100 g/L so red cells push platelets to the vessel wall, and for refractory or recurrent bleeding consider cryoprecipitate or conjugated oestrogens (slower onset, effect over days).

audienceQs.q: PEPTIC and SUP-ICU seemed to show tiny differences. So does the choice of stress-ulcer prophylaxis even matter?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The choice matters less than the selection. PEPTIC (PPI vs H2-blocker) and SUP-ICU (pantoprazole vs placebo) both found small mortality differences in broad ICU populations, which is exactly why the message is to target prophylaxis rather than give it to everyone. Where you do prophylax a genuinely high-risk patient (ventilated ≥48 h or coagulopathic), PPIs prevent clinically important bleeding somewhat more effectively than H2-blockers, but at the cost of a higher infection signal (pneumonia, C. diff) — so it's a trade-off, not a free win. The high-value actions are: prophylax only the right patients, prefer a PPI when you do, feed enterally early, and discontinue the moment the risk factors resolve.

audienceQs.q: A pregnant woman with hyperemesis has haematemesis. Is it safe to scope her, and what's the likely cause?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Yes — upper GI endoscopy is safe in pregnancy when there is a clear indication like significant haematemesis. Use a left-lateral tilt to avoid aortocaval compression, minimise sedation (and involve anaesthetics/obstetrics), and avoid unnecessary radiation. The most likely cause in this setting is a Mallory–Weiss tear from repeated retching in hyperemesis gravidarum; reflux oesophagitis and gastritis are also common, while peptic ulcers are actually less frequent in pregnancy. PPIs are considered safe in pregnancy and are the mainstay, along with treating the hyperemesis and replacing iron. If she had known varices, band ligation would be preferred over sclerotherapy, with fetal monitoring if a non-selective beta-blocker is used.
